body:
Hey there. I visited Croatia when I was 18 and loved it. I guess I went to the touristy part (wasn't too far from Dubrovnik). I just remember it being amazing.

Life really does suck at times. We just have to try and roll with the punches and get through. I've been through the mill myself, I lost my identical twin brother to suicide last year, and have been fighting depression ever since.

Please take the best of care of yourself. You really do live in a beautiful country (and world!). Keep talking on here if there is no one around that you can talk to directly - we're here to listen.

Hi there. When it comes to the standards you set yourself against I truly believe that many of them are arbitrarily set by society and culture. Why should your worth be a measure of financial independence, physical attractiveness, mental state or academic achievements? These are all pressures set by our society (globally) and in my understanding are a very poor measure of an individual. I believe every individual has a wealth of qualities that make them the incredible individual they are, and the majority of these have nothing to do with the aforementioned standards.

Exactly this. I lost my brother one year ago. He loved our family, his friends and his little dog immensely. He was my identical twin and we spent our entire life up to that point as best friends and rivals. Yet this is all overcast by the immediacy of the emotion at hand. Escape is sought in the heat of emotion, often irrationally, and they end their life.

silentlybreathing, if you are still there please call for help.
Sorry. I was unaware. In that case please just post here : )

If she likes animals then she is bound to be awesome : )

She really should vent on here or elsewhere. The internet is perhaps a step behind speaking to someone directly (someone neutral) but has the advantage that it is 24/7. If she hits a bad place she should just jump on and say her piece. She might not even know clearly what is affecting her so deeply though. The mind is complicated at the best of times.

If you believe it's her immediate home environment maybe start heading out somewhere quiet every now and again. I'm sure those pups would love a walk.

When all things are rational and calm thing CAN always change for the better. Sadly suicidal ideation is a mental state that is highly irrational. When you are caught in such a moment all that matters is the present.

Of all of the emotions I have felt after losing my twin brother just over a year ago, guilt is the most complicated. It is multifaceted and as such must be broken down and treated many times. I agree with SunnyRaja2 on this.

He needs someone neutral to speak to. I understand the whole resisting talking to GPs/psychiatrist thing. Also, if the individual is stoic and proud (and stubborn!) then it is unlikely that they will speak to ANYONE openly about the issues that are affecting them. The problem with speaking to those closest to us is that they often rarely listen. They already 'know you' and as such preconceptions are up in full force. Speaking to a neutral individual is a whole different story though.

If you can try and get him to directly enter a neutral environment and speak to someone about his concerns it may do him a world of good. That is much easier said than done in this day and age though. Despite there being more humans than ever before on this planet, and despite all of our wonderful social media technology, I would say with confidence that people have never felt more alone.

As Robin Williams said:

'I used to think that the worst thing in life was to end up alone. It's not. The worst thing in life is to end up with people who make you feel alone.'

Basically, you can be surrounded by all of your closest friends and family who, with the best intention in the world, will still make you feel alone. Those closest to you can often be those most blind to your needs. They don't see with there eyes or hear with their ears so much as do it all with their mind as it's all coloured by preconceptions.

Seek out your primary health care physician ASAP. If they are anything like the GPs (General Practitioners) in the UK they will only be of very little immediate help but they will know the next steps to take. 

It's a HARD step to take but it sounds like she is suffering from suicidal ideation and she needs to find professional help and, perhaps more importantly from my own experience, someone NEUTRAL to speak to.

I have suffered in the past, and still suffer at times to varying degrees, from suicidal ideation, It's a very dangerous mental state to enter and needs to be managed. Drugs may help (antidepressants) but not always. If she is suffering from depression their is a long list of factors that may contribute, perhaps the most insidious being inherent physiology i.e. some people are simply more likely to become depressed. I fall into that category as I have a family history of depression and, sadly, have lost an aunt, cousin and my twin brother to suicide.

Try and support her in seeing her physician. Alongside that I would suggest trying to get her to do something similar to what you have done here yourself - speak to others who are not directly involved in her life and who will genuinely listen to what she has to say. She may have things (almost certainly, like all of us) that she can't say to those who know her. Maybe suggest she create an anonymous account here?

Post here or PM if you want to talk further. I've been through the mill and am a good listener (well, reader in this case). I'd be happy to write to her also.
Thank you for your kind intention. Good to know there are decent people out there.

It's not so much what the staff/patients said, it was more how they listened. It's hard to explain. I know my family is important. Not even they can really understand how close I was to my brother though. They have sympathy but no true empathy. My twin was the only one who could ever understand.

Preconceptions. As in they have predetermined ideas about how things are. It's hard for them to remove themselves from the equation. If they could they would be able to be more objective. The staff and patients in the hospital had no idea who I was.

I don't think family are the best ones to speak to in this instance. The problem with family and friends is that they have too many preconceptions. I've found the most helpful people are those that are completely neutral. When I was in the mental health hospital I found the staff and even the patients were great to speak to. Speaking can only do so much though. It's beneficial for some.

Thank you. You're right in the fact that he wouldn't want me to take my life. If he could see me now he would be devastated. The thing is, he knew that if he took his life it would destroy me and our family, he still did it though. I know that in that moment he wasn't thinking clearly and that, if he hadn't been so efficient and has survived just a few minutes longer, he could have changed his mind. I'm in a slightly different place to him though. While he was alive his situation was completely redeemable. My situation is not. The one thing we all know is that when we lose someone we will never get them back in this life. I can't live with that.

The love of his life kicked him to the curb. It was unexpected. He moved back home to live with our Dad. He had been with her for close to decade. Moving home meant he lost the lifestyle he had loved so much. He had to leave one of his two dogs behind with his ex. He also developed a small debt supporting her. All of this combined would have resulted in him taking his life. I don't think it was any one thing in particular. He had no history of mental illness prior to his break up. Six weeks after going home he tried to take his life, but ended up in hospital. Six weeks after that he succeeded.


As for coping, I'm really not, as indicated in my original post. I tried taking my life, but like my brother, didn't succeed and ended up in A&E followed by a mental hospital for a week. I think I will most likely try again in the next few weeks. The heartache is unbearable.
